A law of the Parliament of Canada, first passed in 1876 and still in force with many changes, that governs registered "Indians", their bands and their reserves. It defines who has Indian status and gives the federal government wide control over First Nations life.

It gathered earlier colonial laws into one, with the aim of assimilating First Nations into settler society. Over the years it and its amendments:

  • set up band councils under the eye of government agents, in place of traditional rule
  • took status away from First Nations women who married non-status men, and their children
  • banned ceremonies such as the potlatch and the sun dance, from 1885 and 1895 until 1951
  • made attendance at residential schools compulsory
  • for many years barred First Nations from hiring lawyers to press land claims

The worst parts were removed in 1951 and 1985, but the Act remains. Many First Nations want it gone, yet fear losing the treaty rights and protections it holds. It was passed under John A. Macdonald's government, which also faced Louis Riel.
